name: The Osage Orange of Marcus Garvey Park

location.address: Southwest corner of Marcus Garvey Park, Harlem, Manhattan

verified_sources: https://www.6sqft.com/the-great-trees-of-nyc-parks-updates-list-for-the-first-time-in-40-years/

transport: Subway 2/3 at 125th St (Lenox Av), a short walk
story: This Osage orange in Harlem has ended up in an art exhibition. Its twisting, wraparound trunk is referenced in Tree Reflections, a public art piece by Susan Stair that was shown at Conference House Park on Staten Island, a whole borough and a ferry ride away from the tree itself. That trunk is the reason to come. The local press coverage of the 2024 Great Trees list singled out its unique twisting form, and the Parks listing describes the trunk as wrapping around itself. It measures 58 inches across, about 4.6 metres round, and the city's forestry inventory gives exactly the same figure for the only Osage orange that size in the park. The inventory found it in Good condition in May 2026. NYC Parks added it to the Great Trees list in October 2024, when the city updated its roll of remarkable trees for the first time in about forty years. The description of the trunk reaches us through press coverage of the Parks listing, so treat it as second-hand. The measurement and the location come straight from the city's own inventory. It stands at the southwest corner of Marcus Garvey Park, free public parkland in the middle of Harlem. Nobody has dated it. If you know when it went in, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the twisting trunk that wraps around itself, 58 inches across. It stands at the southwest corner of Marcus Garvey Park in Harlem.

name: The American Elm of Mapes Park

location.address: Mapes Park, near East 180th Street and Mapes Avenue, Bronx

verified_sources: https://www.6sqft.com/the-great-trees-of-nyc-parks-updates-list-for-the-first-time-in-40-years/

transport: Subway 2/5 at East 180th St, a few minutes' walk
story: When Mapes Park in the Bronx was rebuilt, the neighbours made sure this elm came through it. The press coverage of the 2024 Great Trees list says the tree inspired the neighbourhood to push for its preservation during the park renovations, and the Parks listing credits community members, working through the city's Community Parks Initiative, with protecting it. The park's ballfield was rebuilt under that same initiative in 2021. The tree the neighbours stood up for is worth the trip. Its trunk measures 62 inches across, about five metres round, which is large for an American elm growing in a city. It is also the only American elm of any real size in the park; the city's forestry inventory lists no other above 30 inches, and its 62 inch entry matches the Great Tree figure exactly. That inventory found it in Good condition in February 2026. NYC Parks added it to the Great Trees list in October 2024, putting a tree its neighbours had defended onto the city's roll of its most remarkable trees. The description reaches us through press coverage of the Parks listing, so treat the details as second-hand; the measurement and the location are the city's own. It stands in Mapes Park near East 180th Street and Mapes Avenue, free public parkland. Nobody has dated it. If you know when it was planted, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, 62 inches across, the one big American elm in the park. It stands in Mapes Park near East 180th Street and Mapes Avenue in the Bronx.

name: The Sycamore of Morningside Park

location.address: Morningside Park, beside a path fork just north of the West 120th Street entrance, Manhattan

verified_sources: https://www.westsiderag.com/2024/10/09/parks-releases-new-map-of-citys-great-trees-eight-of-them-are-in-central-park
https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/hn5i-inap.json (Forestry Tree Points: Platanus occidentalis, dbh 48 in, Full/Good, record dated 2017-04-19)

access: Free; public city park (steep slope park; stay on paths)
transport: Subway 1 at 116th St-Columbia University or B/C at 116th St, about 10 minutes' walk
verify_notes: West Side Rag (fetched): the only new Manhattan addition in the Oct 2024 list, an American sycamore just north of West 120th Street in Morningside Park. Parks listing (search result, page bot-blocked): trunk diameter 48 in, next to a path fork north of the W 120th St entrance. Pin: the only American sycamore >=20 in dbh in the park in the forestry points, dbh 48 equals the Great Tree figure; plain-sycamore (Platanus occidentalis) is distinct from the London planes around it. Alive: Great Tree designation Oct 2024; forestry record itself dated 2017 (Good), so no fresh independent observation. Height not found. Age not documented. Flagged.
story:
When New York's parks department revised its list of Great Trees in October 2024, the first revision in about forty years, Manhattan got exactly one new entry. It was this American sycamore in Morningside Park, standing beside a fork in the path just north of the West 120th Street entrance.

Its trunk is 48 inches across, about 3.8 metres round, and the city's forestry inventory rated it in good condition at its last inspection. It is also easy to overlook. New York is full of London planes, the hybrid that is the city's most common street tree, and this tree's parent species looks much like them at a glance. The plain American sycamore is the native one, the tree of eastern river valleys, and in Morningside it is the only one of its size.

The park itself is a long, steep strip of rock between Harlem below and Morningside Heights above, laid out in the late nineteenth century to deal with a cliff too sheer for streets. The sycamore grows in that park, with the Columbia campus a few blocks west on the heights and the subway a ten-minute walk away.

Nobody has published its height, its age or when it was planted, and the forestry record dates from 2017. If you know more, or have stood under it lately, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the one native American sycamore among the London planes, its trunk about 3.8 metres round. It stands beside the path fork just north of the West 120th Street entrance.

story:
A fire in the 1970s left a gap on East 6th Street, and a weeping willow now taller than six storeys fills it. After the blaze the city cleared the burnt tenement and set the lot aside for community gardening. The Creative Little Garden opened in 1978 and has been run by volunteers ever since, and its willow, according to Village View's 2024 profile, spreads a canopy about 12 metres across over a blue stone patio.

In 2024 the parks department put the tree on its list of Great Trees, the first new additions in about forty years. Its measurements depend on who held the tape. The 2024 listing gives the trunk as 37 inches across. The city's forestry inventory, updated in July 2026, gives 42, about 3.35 metres round. The willow may simply have grown, or the two were measured at different heights.

By one account the willow was planted in 1978 as a community effort, the same year the garden opened. That date is reported rather than confirmed, so treat it as likely rather than settled. If you were there when it went in, tell us.

For a weeping willow in Manhattan, a tree that likes wet ground and open sky, to reach this size on a former tenement lot is the surprise. The garden opens at posted hours only, so check before going. Another big willow, in El Jardin del Paraiso, stands about 450 metres east, which makes a two-garden walk.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the weeping crown over the blue stone patio, more than six storeys high. It stands in the Creative Little Garden at 530 East 6th Street.

name: The Dawn Redwood of the Liz Christy Garden

location.address: Liz Christy Community Garden, Bowery and East Houston Street, Manhattan

verified_sources: https://villageview.nyc/2024/12/04/great-trees-of-new-york-city/

transport: B/D/F/M at Broadway-Lafayette St or 6 at Bleecker St, about 5 minutes' walk
verify_notes: Village View (fetched): dawn redwood planted in 1981 by Tessa Huxley, about 100 ft tall, visible along Houston Street from Avenue B to Greene Street; Huxley recalled scraping the top of the subway tunnel digging the hole; noticeably cooler beneath it. Garden is the city's first community garden (Liz Christy, 1973: not checked here). Age is a documented planting date (45 years). Pin: the only dawn redwood in the surrounding forestry points, dbh 30 in, record dated 2019; kept approximate because only one source gives the height and the Parks page was not fetched. The Parks Great Trees page id unknown (no page reached). Flagged.
story:
When Tessa Huxley dug the hole for this tree in 1981, she scraped the top of the subway tunnel. The dawn redwood she planted in the Liz Christy Community Garden, at the Bowery and East Houston Street, now stands about 30 metres tall. You can pick it out along Houston Street from Avenue B all the way to Greene Street, a conifer rising over the low roofs, and it is noticeably cooler underneath.

The species has a stranger history than most. Dawn redwood was first described from fossils, and scientists assumed it was long extinct until living trees turned up in central China in the 1940s. Seed reached American gardens at the end of that decade. So a tree that the textbooks had buried grows here over a subway line, forty-five years after a volunteer put it in the ground.

That makes it young for a tree on New York's Great Trees list, which the parks department revised in 2024. It also makes its story unusually complete, down to the year, the gardener and what lay under the spade. For most old trees in this city, nobody wrote any of that down.

The garden is run by volunteers and opens only at posted hours, so check before going. The tree does not need the gate to be open. It is in view from Houston Street.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by its height, a conifer about 30 metres tall standing over the low buildings, the only dawn redwood on the block. It stands inside the Liz Christy Community Garden at the Bowery and East Houston Street.

name: The White Ash of Van Cortlandt Park

location.address: East side of the entrance to the cross-country trail, Van Cortlandt Park, Bronx

verified_sources: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/hn5i-inap.json (Forestry Tree Points: Fraxinus americana, dbh 60 in, Full/Fair, updated 2026-05-31)
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/User:Found5dollar/Great_Trees_of_New_York_City (draft that transcribes the Parks entry: 82.8 ft, 56.6 in, 60.5 ft spread; not an authority)

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees (1985 list, id 23)

transport: Subway 1 to Van Cortlandt Park-242nd St, about 15 minutes' walk
story: This white ash has been cloned, and its copy grows elsewhere in the same park, at the south end of Van Cortlandt Park's Parade Ground. The original is the one worth the walk. It was on NYC Parks' first Great Trees list in 1985, and it is still alive in the years of the emerald ash borer, which has made a white ash this size a rare thing to find standing at all. The numbers have grown since that first list. In 1985 it measured 56.6 inches across the trunk and 82.8 feet tall. Parks now gives about 60 inches, nearly 4.8 metres round, and the city's forestry inventory, updated in May 2026, agrees on the 60 inches. That same record grades it Fair rather than Good, so this is a survivor, not an untouched one. It stands on the east side of the entrance to Van Cortlandt Park's cross-country trail, free public parkland in the Bronx. There is a second large ash within a hundred metres, at about 40 inches, so check the trunk; the big one is half as thick again. The Red Horse Chestnut of Van Cortlandt House is in the same park, which makes a two-tree walk. Two caveats on the sources. The 1985 figures come to us through a transcription of the Parks list, not the Parks page itself, and nobody has published an age. If you know it, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about 60 inches across, half as thick again as the 40 inch ash nearby. It stands on the east side of the entrance to the cross-country trail in Van Cortlandt Park.

name: The American Elm of Crotona Park

location.address: Crotona Park, near the Claremont Parkway entrance on Crotona Park East, Bronx

verified_sources: https://www.6sqft.com/the-great-trees-of-nyc-parks-updates-list-for-the-first-time-in-40-years/
https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/hn5i-inap.json (Forestry Tree Points: Ulmus americana, dbh 52 in, Full/Fair, updated 2026-07-20)

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees (2024 addition, id 68)

transport: Bronx subway 2/5 serves the park's east side; check the exact stop
story: No other elm in Crotona Park comes close. The city's forestry survey counts this American elm at 52 inches across the trunk, roughly four metres round, and finds no second elm in the park that reaches 50. In 2024 NYC Parks put it on its list of Great Trees, the first time that list had been updated in about forty years, which puts this corner of the Bronx on the city's official roll of its finest trees. The Parks listing places it on the north side, near the entrance where Claremont Parkway meets Crotona Park East. That is about all the official record says. Nobody has published a height, and nobody has published an age, so we will not invent one. What the record does say is that the tree is alive. The forestry survey updated its entry in July 2026 and logged it in full leaf and fair condition, the bookkeeper's version of still standing and still working. One honest caveat about the map. Our pin sits on the forestry point that matches the size, the only elm that large in the park, but we could not confirm that it lines up exactly with the entrance the Parks listing names, so treat it as close rather than exact and look for the biggest elm on that side. If you know when it was planted, or have walked past it for decades, tell us.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the trunk, about four metres round, larger than any other elm in the park. It stands on the north side, near the Claremont Parkway entrance on Crotona Park East.

access: Community garden; open only at posted garden hours, check before going (hours not verified)
transport: L train to 1st Av, about 12 minutes' walk
story: This is a willow with a school timetable. Children from the nearby New Amsterdam School climb it, and since 2011 a New School class in community gardening has met beneath it, so this is a working tree rather than an ornament. It grows in El Jardin del Paraiso on East 5th Street, described by the local paper Village View as the neighbourhood's largest community garden, and in 2024 NYC Parks added it to its list of Great Trees. The city's forestry survey puts this one at 41 inches across the trunk, a little over three metres round, which is very large for its kind on a Manhattan block. Village View credits the planting to Liz Christy, years ago, without a year, and no other source we found dates it. So its age stays open. If you were there when it went in, tell us. Two practical notes. The garden is a community garden, not a park, so it opens only at its posted hours; check before you go. And our pin is approximate, since we could not confirm the forestry point sits inside the garden fence. Once you are at the garden gate, though, there is no other willow to mistake it for.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it as the big weeping willow inside El Jardin del Paraiso, a trunk a little over three metres round. It stands in the community garden on East 5th Street, the only large willow on the block.

name: The Elms of the Heather Garden Promenade

location.address: Stan Michels Promenade above the Heather Garden, Fort Tryon Park, Manhattan

verified_sources: https://forttryonpark.org/american-elm-trees/
https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/hn5i-inap.json (Forestry Tree Points: two American elms near the promenade, dbh 59 in updated 2026-09-02 and 54 in updated 2024-08-06, both Full/Good)
transport: A train to 190th St, then a short walk; or 1 train to 191st St
story: Every other year, someone injects these elms with medicine. The Fort Tryon Park Trust pays to inoculate 48 American elms in the park against Dutch elm disease, because many of the original trees have already died. The survivors on the Stan Michels Promenade are the park's best-known. The Trust describes the park's elms as more than a hundred years old, planted widely in the early 1900s. That is a date for the planting as a whole, not a birth certificate for any one tree, so read it as over a century and probably not by much more. The promenade runs above the Heather Garden, which the Trust gives as opening in 1935, and the elms line it. The one people mention most stands at the northern end, its low branches reaching out over the garden beds. The city's forestry survey finds the two biggest American elms in the park here, 59 and 54 inches across the trunk, about 70 metres apart. The larger works out at nearly five metres round. We cannot yet say which of the two is the northern-end tree, so this entry is the pair, and our pin sits on one of them rather than a proven favourite. Both were logged in full leaf and good condition. Walk the promenade end to end and you have seen both, along with what a century of careful nursing looks like.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise them as the two largest elms on the Stan Michels Promenade, the bigger nearly five metres round. They stand about 70 metres apart above the Heather Garden; the most-cited one is at the northern end.

name: The Ginkgo of the Cloisters Lawn

location.address: South end of the Cloisters Lawn, Fort Tryon Park, Manhattan

verified_sources: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/resource/hn5i-inap.json (Forestry Tree Points: Ginkgo biloba, dbh 52 in, Full/Good, updated 2025-02-19)
NYC Parks Great Trees listing, seen only as a search-result snippet: ginkgo at the south end of the Cloisters Lawn, 48 in trunk diameter

official_register.name: NYC Parks Great Trees (2024 list; entry id not found)

access: Free; the lawn is public park (the Cloisters museum itself is separate and ticketed)
transport: A train to 190th St then bus or walk through the park, or 1 train to 191st St; about 15 minutes' walk
story: The Cloisters charges for entry; the Great Tree on its lawn does not. This ginkgo stands at the south end of the Cloisters Lawn in Fort Tryon Park, and NYC Parks includes it in its 2024 list of Great Trees. Its trunk is around four metres round. The two measurements we have disagree slightly, 48 inches across in the Parks listing and 52 in the city's forestry survey, a gap that ordinary growth between surveys or a different tape position easily explains. Either way it is one of only two ginkgos in the park with a trunk over 20 inches; the other stands about 450 metres south, near the Heather Garden. Nobody has published when this one was planted, so its age is an open question. If you know, tell us. The forestry survey logged it alive and in good condition in February 2025. The lawn is ordinary public park, open to anyone walking through Fort Tryon, and the museum is a separate visit. Our pin sits on the forestry point nearest the lawn, which we think is the Great Tree but have not proven, so it is marked approximate. Come in November, when ginkgos turn gold all at once and then drop their leaves within a day or two.
how_to_recognise: You can recognise it by the fan-shaped leaves and a trunk about four metres round, far bigger than any ginkgo nearby. It stands at the south end of the Cloisters Lawn, outside the museum.
